english.title: Possess pyrotechnic article at a protest
english.standardoffencewording:
On **(..SPECIFY DATE..) at **(..SPECIFY TOWNSHIP..) possessed a pyrotechnic article namely, **(..SPECIFY PYROTECHNIC ARTICLE..), at a time when you were taking part in a

(A)_[public procession constituting a,]_
(B)_[public assembly constituting a,]_
(C)_[one-person]_

english.legislation: Contrary to section 160 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026.

english.notes:
(i)“One-person protest” has the meaning given by section 14ZA(4) of the Public Order Act 1986; “public assembly” and “public procession” have the meanings given by section 16 of that Act.(ii) A “pyrotechnic article” is defined in section 160(7) as an article that contains explosive substances or an explosive mixture of substances designed to produce heat, light, sound, gas or smoke (or a combination of such effects) through self-sustained exothermic chemical reaction. Matches and certain articles specified by the Secretary of State in regulations aren't covered by the definition.
(iii) Section 160(2) provides this offence won't be committed by a person taking part in a cultural or religious event of a kind at which pyrotechnic articles are customarily used. This would cover, for example, events celebrating Chinese New Year or Diwali. (iv) Sections 160(3) and 160(4) of the 2026 Act provide a defence of reasonable excuse for possession. In particular, where a person is in possession of the item in connection with their work. (v) Other offences restrict or prohibit pyrotechnic use in specific circumstances. For example, section 54 of the Metropolitan Police Act 1839 prohibits the throwing or setting fire to fireworks in throughfares or public places within the limits of the Metropolitan Police District and section 80 of the Explosives Act 1875 makes it an offence to throw, cast or fire a firework in a street or public place.
